meta.tagline: The French Riviera's real city — not the postcard, the place

pills: The beach is pebbles, not sand
Climb the hill, skip the lift

overview.title: Welcome to Nice
overview.intro: Nice isn't Monaco. It isn't a film set, a yacht show, or a luxury showcase. It's a real Mediterranean city — Italy-flavoured, sun-drenched, and entirely itself. The fifth largest city in France and the capital of the French Riviera, Nice has been seducing visitors since the 18th century when English aristocrats wintered here to escape the cold, eventually building the seafront promenade that still bears their name. But the Nice worth discovering is older and quieter than any promenade: Vieux Nice, the ochre and terracotta old town, with its Baroque churches, flower market, and lanes so narrow they block out the sky. The socca seller who's been at the same corner for forty years. The midday cannon that has fired from Castle Hill every day since 1861. This city has its own language, its own food, and a pride that has nothing to do with the people who come here in summer.

local_word.definition: Nice's street food, its soul food, its oldest food. A thin, crispy pancake made from chickpea flour, olive oil, and water — baked in a wood-fired oven on a huge copper plate, cut into irregular wedges, served hot with black pepper. Nothing else. No cheese, no toppings, no variations. Eaten standing at a market stall, in paper, while still too hot. Chez Thérésa at Cours Saleya has been making it since the 1920s. This is where you start.

rules.title: The beach is pebbles — and the locals love it that way
rules.description: Nice's famous beach is made of smooth, rounded pebbles, not sand. There is no sand anywhere on the main beach. This surprises almost every first-time visitor. Bring beach shoes, rent a mat from one of the private beach operators, or do what locals do and find a flat stone. The upside: the water is extraordinarily clear and the beach never feels gritty.

rules.title: Nice is not Provence — and not fully French
rules.description: Nice was Italian until 1860, formally ceded to France by Napoleon III. The old town architecture, the food, the dialect (Niçard), and the character of the place all carry that Italian imprint. The local word for Nice in the old dialect is Nissa. This is not a French city that happens to be near Italy; it's a Mediterranean city that is both, and entirely neither.

rules.title: Castle Hill — always on foot, always free
rules.description: Colline du Château rises 92 metres above the city and offers the best view in Nice: the curve of the Baie des Anges, the orange rooftops of Vieux Nice, the Alps in the distance. There's a lift, but walk up — the staircase through the rock is part of the experience, and the descent through Vieux Nice rewards you immediately. Free, always. One of the great free views in Europe.

tip.label: The midday cannon
tip.text: Every day at noon, a cannon fires from Castle Hill. It has fired every day since 1861. Legend has it that a Scottish lord named Sir Thomas Coventry, tired of his wife returning late from shopping in town, persuaded the city council to fire a cannon at midday so she would know to come home. Nice kept doing it for over 160 years. If you're in the city at noon, stop what you're doing and listen.

transport.title: Getting Around
transport.intro: Nice is compact, walkable, and well-connected. The tram handles most of what you need; your feet handle the rest. The city is also the perfect base for the entire French Riviera by train.

items.title: Airport (NCE) → City Centre
items.description: Tram line 2 connects the airport directly to the city centre in about 10 minutes — one of the best airport connections in France. Runs frequently, stops at Place Masséna and Vieux Nice. Taxis are significantly more expensive and traffic-dependent. The tram is always the right choice.

items.title: Trams — the city's main network
items.description: Nice has two tram lines. Line 1 runs east-west through the city centre connecting the main neighbourhoods. Line 2 connects the airport to the port and city centre. A single ticket is valid for 74 minutes on all tram and bus lines — validate on board every time. A 24-hour pass is good value if you're making three or more trips. Buy tickets at machines at tram stops.

items.title: Train — for day trips along the Riviera
items.description: Nice Ville station is one of France's best-connected coastal stations. Monaco is 25 minutes. Antibes 30 minutes. Cannes 40 minutes. Menton and the Italian border 45 minutes. Trains run frequently and are the most scenic way to see the Riviera coast — the line hugs the coast and the views alone are worth the ticket. Far cheaper and more reliable than driving.

items.title: Vélo Bleu — city bike share
items.description: Nice's public bike-share scheme has stations throughout the city. A short-term subscription gives access to the bikes; the first 30 minutes is included. The Promenade des Anglais has a dedicated bike lane running the full 7km — one of the best urban cycling routes in France. Best for the Promenade, the port area, and the flat parts of the city.

items.title: On foot — the only way for Vieux Nice
items.description: Vieux Nice cannot be explored any other way — the lanes are too narrow for vehicles, and half the best things are unmarked. The old town is 15 minutes' walk from Place Masséna. Castle Hill is 20 minutes from the old town on foot. The Promenade des Anglais is 7km end to end and completely flat. Nice rewards walking above all else.

callout.label: Day trip strategy
callout.text: Nice makes an exceptional base. Use the train freely: Monaco on Tuesday for the market; Antibes on a quiet afternoon; Èze village at sunset by bus then train back. The Riviera is compact — a different town every day is entirely possible without ever moving your bag.

stay.title: Where to Stay
stay.intro: Nice's neighbourhoods are small, walkable, and very different in character. The right one depends entirely on what kind of city you want.

local_word.definition: The old town — the real heart of the city. A dense grid of narrow lanes between the Promenade and Castle Hill, painted in every shade of ochre, terracotta, and faded yellow. Baroque churches appear around every corner. The Cours Saleya market fills the main square every morning. At night the restaurants and bars take over. Staying in Vieux Nice means waking up inside the city's soul.

items.name: Vieux Nice (Old Town)
items.description: The historic quarter — baroque churches, the flower market, narrow lanes, great restaurants. The most beautiful place to stay in the city. Lively at night. Some streets can be noisy on weekends. But nowhere else puts you so completely inside what makes Nice worth visiting.

items.name: Promenade des Anglais
items.description: The seafront boulevard. Grand Belle Époque hotels, the legendary Negresco, the sea on one side and the city on the other. Expensive, iconic, and everything the French Riviera promises. Slightly removed from the city's daily life — more resort than neighbourhood — but the morning walk along the water is hard to beat.

items.name: Le Port & Garibaldi
items.description: The eastern quarter around the port — colourful, genuinely local, and largely undiscovered by tourists. The best restaurants in Nice are concentrated here. Place Garibaldi is one of the city's most beautiful squares. Slightly further from the beach but connected by tram. Where Niçois actually go out to eat.

items.name: Musiciens Quarter & Libération
items.description: The residential neighbourhoods north of the train station — Belle Époque apartment buildings, local markets, excellent neighbourhood cafés, none of the tourist premium. Well connected by tram. Where Nice residents actually live. Libération market on Tuesday and Friday mornings is outstanding.

best_time.title: Best Time to Visit
best_time.intro: Nice has over 300 days of sunshine per year. Every season offers something different — the real question is which crowds and which version of the city you want.

items.label: Spring
items.name: Perfect Season
items.subtitle: Spring · The Best Time
items.description: April and May are when Nice is most itself. The light is extraordinary, the crowds haven't arrived, the markets are overflowing with spring produce, and every terrace is open. By April, the hills behind the city are green and the mimosa is in bloom. The sea is still too cold for swimming but the Promenade in the morning light is one of the great urban walks in Europe. By May the city is at its quietest and most beautiful — museums empty, restaurants bookable, the lanes of Vieux Nice belonging entirely to the people who live there.

callout.label: Spring timing tip
callout.text: If late April coincides with Milan's Salone del Mobile, Nice makes a perfect base — the two cities are 4.5 hours apart by train and easily combined in a single trip. Nice prices haven't risen yet, the crowds haven't arrived, and the weather is ideal.

items.label: Summer
items.name: Peak Riviera
items.subtitle: Summer · Glorious and Crowded
items.description: July and August are when the world comes to Nice. The beaches are packed, the restaurants are full, the sea is warm and clear, and the city buzzes with an energy that's hard to find elsewhere. But it comes at a price: everything costs more, queues are longer, and the real Nice retreats behind the tourist season. July brings the Festival du Jazz de Nice in Cimiez park — one of France's great outdoor festivals, under the olive trees where Matisse is buried.

callout.label: 14 July — fireworks over the Baie des Anges
callout.text: Bastille Day in Nice is one of the most spectacular in France. Fireworks are launched along the Promenade des Anglais and reflect off the Baie des Anges — the entire city comes down to the seafront. The Jazz Festival also runs in July at Cimiez park, under the olive trees next to Matisse's grave. Two of the south of France's great summer events, in the same city, in the same month.

items.label: Autumn
items.name: Best Kept Secret
items.subtitle: Autumn · The Real Secret
items.description: September and October are the best-kept secret of the French Riviera. The crowds drop sharply after August, the sea stays warm enough to swim until mid-October, and the city returns to its daily rhythm. Restaurant prices normalise, tables are easier to book, and the light takes on a golden quality. November brings the first rains but also the first fires in the fireplaces of Vieux Nice's trattorias. The town belongs to itself again.

callout.label: Local secret
callout.text: The sea in Nice is swimmable until at least mid-October, sometimes longer. September at Coco Beach — the locals' favourite hidden cove — with almost no tourists, warm water, and golden light. The best single day Nice offers.

items.label: Winter
items.name: Mild & Quiet
items.subtitle: Winter · Europe's Sunniest Winter City
items.description: Nice is genuinely mild in winter — average January temperatures around 13°C, and the sun appears regularly even in the coldest months. This is why the English came in the first place. The Promenade des Anglais on a sunny December morning, nearly empty, with the Alps visible behind the city, is one of the most quietly beautiful urban experiences in Europe. Prices drop significantly. Locals take over. The old town is at its most authentic.

callout.label: Come for the Carnival
callout.text: Carnaval de Nice (February): one of the world's great carnivals, dating to 1294. The Battle of Flowers alone is worth planning a trip for — flower-covered floats and bouquets thrown into the crowd. In winter Nice is at its most affordable and most local; the Carnival transforms it entirely for two weeks. Book accommodation many months ahead.

monthly_highlights.text: Nice Carnival: France's biggest carnival — two weeks of flower battles (bataille de fleurs) and giant puppets.
A double feast next door: the Cannes Film Festival and the Monaco GP; Nice is the base for both, hotels fill early.
Nice Jazz Festival: summer nights of jazz at the Théâtre de Verdure and Masséna; Europe's oldest jazz festival.
The secret season: the sea still warm, the crowds gone, the light a painter's light. Nice at its best.

eat.title: What to Eat
eat.intro: Niçoise cuisine is one of France's most distinct regional traditions — Mediterranean, olive-based, deeply vegetable-driven, and largely ignored by the rest of the country. This is the food of a city that was Italian until 1860 and has never entirely forgotten it.

local_word.definition: The drink of the south. An anise-flavoured spirit, served with a small jug of cold water to dilute. The water turns it milky and opaque — that's correct, not a mistake. Ricard is the standard brand; ask for Pastis de Nice for the local version. Ordered at any bar from about 6pm onwards, particularly on Cours Saleya. Skip the beer; drink what the locals drink.

items.name: Socca — start here, always
items.description: Chickpea flour, olive oil, water, salt. Baked in a wood-fired oven at very high heat on a huge copper plate until the edges are crisp and the centre yielding. Cut into wedges, served immediately, eaten with black pepper. Chez Thérésa at Cours Saleya has been making it since the 1920s — arrive before 10am or queue. Socca is unique to Nice and this area; it doesn't exist anywhere else in France.
items.tag: Chez Thérésa · Cours Saleya · arrive early

items.name: Pan Bagnat — Nice's great sandwich
items.description: A round country bread soaked in olive oil, then filled with tuna, hard-boiled egg, raw vegetables, anchovies, olives, and black pepper. The bread must absorb the oil for at least an hour before eating — it is not a fast food item but a patient one. Chez TinTin near Cours Saleya is consistently voted the best in the city. The perfect lunch to take to Castle Hill.
items.tag: Chez TinTin · eat it overlooking the sea

items.name: Salade Niçoise — the real one
items.description: Raw vegetables only: tomato, cucumber, radish, spring onion, green pepper, broad beans. Hard-boiled egg. Good tuna in oil. Anchovy fillets. Black olives. Dressed with olive oil. No cooked vegetables, no lettuce, no green beans unless very young and raw. The Nice Tourism Board has a registered recipe. Any restaurant serving it with cooked green beans is lying to you.
items.tag: Raw vegetables only · no cooked green beans

items.name: Pissaladière — the original pizza
items.description: Thick, soft bread dough topped with a deeply caramelised onion compote, black olives, and anchovy fillets — nothing else. Sold by the slice in boulangeries throughout Vieux Nice. Eaten standing up, warm, with a coffee. The onions must cook for at least an hour; the result is sweet, savoury, and entirely addictive. The predecessor of all pizza.
items.tag: Sold in every Vieux Nice bakery · warm, by the slice

items.name: Bellet wine — Nice's best-kept secret
items.description: Almost nobody outside Nice knows this exists: a tiny AOC wine appellation in the hills directly above the city, producing red, white, and rosé. Only about 50 hectares of vines. The rosé is exceptional and almost impossible to find outside the region. Look for it on wine lists throughout the city — it's local, it's rare, and it's very good.
items.tag: AOC Bellet · local and rare · ask for it

items.name: Coffee — the Italian way
items.description: Nice's Italian heritage shows in its coffee culture. Espresso is drunk standing at the bar, short and strong. A noisette is espresso with a dash of warm milk — the local standard. Cappuccino exists but is a morning-only drink. The cafés on Cours Saleya are tourist-priced; the cafés one street back in Vieux Nice are where locals go. The difference in price and quality is immediate.
items.tag: Stand at the bar · noisette is the local order

callout.label: Cours Saleya — morning ritual
callout.text: The flower and food market at Cours Saleya runs Tuesday to Sunday until early afternoon. Get there before 9am: the light is extraordinary, the socca is fresh, the flower sellers are arranging their stalls, and you're sharing it with Niçois rather than tourists. Buy flowers. Eat socca. Drink a coffee. This is the best morning in Nice.

hidden_gems.title: Hidden Gems
hidden_gems.intro: Nice hides its best things in plain sight — on a hillside everyone walks past, in a cove everyone misses, behind a church door that's always open. The rewards for the curious are extraordinary.

items.rarity: Where Hitchcock filmed — and Grace Kelly changed her life
items.name: To Catch a Thief locations — the Grande Corniche
items.description: Hitchcock filmed To Catch a Thief (1955) on the French Riviera — the Promenade des Anglais, the mountain roads of the Grande Corniche, and the gardens of Monaco. The film starred Cary Grant and Grace Kelly, and the chemistry between them reportedly led to Grace Kelly meeting Prince Rainier of Monaco shortly afterwards at the Cannes Film Festival. She flew out of Nice airport as a commoner for the last time in 1956. The Corniche road Hitchcock used is still there — same curves, same views, same light.

items.rarity: The locals' beach — no tourists, no crowds
items.name: Coco Beach — east of the Port
items.description: Just past the port, east along the coast, a rocky path leads to Coco Beach — a small, sheltered cove of flat rocks and extraordinarily clear water. No facilities, no beach clubs, no hawkers. Just Niçois who have been coming here for generations. The coastal path continues from here, hugging the cliff face for 1.4km with views out over the Baie des Anges. In winter the path catches the low sun and is one of the most beautiful walks in the city.

items.rarity: A Russian cathedral in the middle of Nice
items.name: Cathédrale Saint-Nicolas — Avenue Nicolas II
items.description: Six onion domes, colourful mosaics, and the largest Russian Orthodox cathedral in Western Europe — standing in a quiet garden ten minutes from the Promenade. Built in 1912 with the support of Tsar Nicholas II, for the large Russian aristocratic community that wintered in Nice. The Romanovs had strong connections to the city; Tsarevich Nicholas died here in 1865. The interior is extraordinary and almost unknown to most visitors. Free entry.

items.rarity: Matisse's grave — under olive trees, in a Roman park
items.name: Monastère de Cimiez — Cimiez Hill
items.description: Henri Matisse lived in Nice for the last 37 years of his life and is buried in the cemetery of the Monastère de Cimiez, alongside fellow artist Raoul Dufy. The monastery sits in a Roman archaeological park — the ruins of a Roman amphitheatre, an olive grove, and a public garden where locals play pétanque. The Musée Matisse is next door and houses the world's largest Matisse collection. Almost no tourist map connects all three. Walk up. Take time.

items.rarity: Nice's secret vineyard — above the city
items.name: AOC Bellet — the hills of Saint-Roman-de-Bellet
items.description: In the hills directly above Nice, largely invisible from the city, a tiny wine appellation produces some of the most interesting wine in the south of France. AOC Bellet covers only about 50 hectares and produces red, white, and rosé — most of it consumed locally, almost none exported. The rosé is exceptional. Several domaines offer visits by appointment. Ask in any wine shop for Bellet — the reaction of the person behind the counter will tell you whether they know anything about wine.

items.rarity: The cannon you won't hear coming
items.name: Le Canon du Midi — Castle Hill
items.description: Every day at exactly noon, a cannon fires from Castle Hill. It has done so every day since 1861. The story: a Scottish lord named Sir Thomas Coventry, impatient for his wife to return from shopping in town, persuaded the Nice city council to fire a cannon at midday so she would know to come home. The city kept doing it for over 160 years. Walk up to Castle Hill before noon — you can watch the firing from close range, and the view from the top is the best in Nice.

callout.label: Anyone can walk into the Negresco
callout.text: Le Negresco has been the most iconic building on the Promenade des Anglais since 1913. You don't need to be a guest — walk in, order a drink at Le Versailles bar, and sit on the terrace overlooking the sea. The legendary interior dome and art-filled salons are free to admire. One of the world's great hotel interiors, no reservation required.

checklist.title: Nice Checklist
checklist.completion_message: Magnifique! You found the real Nice.

items.label: Eat socca at Chez Thérésa — Cours Saleya, before 10am
items.sub: Chickpea flour, wood-fired oven, black pepper. The only socca that matters. Arrive early.

items.label: Walk Cours Saleya market at dawn
items.sub: Tuesday to Sunday. Flowers, food, socca, coffee. Niçois before the tourists. The best morning in Nice.

items.label: Climb Castle Hill on foot — never take the lift
items.sub: 92 metres. The staircase through the rock. The cannon at noon. The best free view in Nice.

items.label: Walk the Sentier du Littoral from Coco Beach
items.sub: 1.4km of coastal path east of the port. Locals only. Extraordinary views. No crowds.

items.label: Eat a Pan Bagnat at Chez TinTin
items.sub: The Nice sandwich. Olive oil-soaked bread, tuna, egg, anchovies. Take it to the hill.

items.label: Walk the Promenade des Anglais at sunrise
items.sub: 7km, flat, free. The sea, the city, the light. Before anyone else arrives.

items.label: Find the Cathédrale Saint-Nicolas
items.sub: Six Russian onion domes in a Nice garden. Built for the Romanovs. Almost no one visits.

items.label: Climb to Cimiez — Matisse's grave and the Roman ruins
items.sub: Monastery garden, Roman amphitheatre, olive trees, pétanque. Musée Matisse next door.

items.label: Order Bellet wine at a local restaurant
items.sub: AOC from the hills above Nice. Ask for it. Almost no one outside Nice knows it exists.

items.label: Drive or walk the Grande Corniche — Hitchcock's road
items.sub: The mountain road above the city. Used in To Catch a Thief (1955). The view hasn't changed.

items.label: Be in Nice at noon — listen for the cannon
items.sub: Castle Hill, every day since 1861. You'll hear it wherever you are in the city.

items.label: Take the train to Villefranche-sur-Mer for a morning
items.sub: 8 minutes from Nice Ville. One of the most beautiful bays in Europe. Almost no facilities. Perfect.

traps.title: Skip the Traps
traps.intro: Nice is small but its tourism is big; the traps cluster along the seafront. Know these four and enjoy the Mediterranean like a local.

items.name: Beach clubs charging for everything
items.description: At the private beaches on the Promenade, sunbed plus umbrella plus towel adds up to hotel money — and the pebbles are the same pebbles.
items.instead: Use the public beach: lay your towel, swim the same sea. If you want comfort, ask for the price list before sitting down.

items.name: 'Menu touristique' on the edges of Cours Saleya
items.description: Some restaurants on the tourist side of the flower market run on photo menus and frozen 'Niçoise' classics.
items.instead: Buy from the market itself, or walk two streets in: real pissaladière waits in the small eateries of Vieux Nice.

items.name: Socca that isn't served hot
items.description: Socca is eaten the moment it leaves the oven; pre-cooked, microwaved socca is an injustice to the city.
items.instead: Choose where it goes straight from wood fire to plate (Chez Pipo is the classic); lots of black pepper, eat with your hands.

items.name: Driving the coast in summer
items.description: In July and August the corniche is a parking war plus traffic; a rental car is usually a burden, not freedom.
items.instead: Take the train: Villefranche, Èze, Monaco, Cannes are all on the coastal line. The view comes free.

callout.label: The golden rule
callout.text: Most of Nice's beauty is free: the sea, the light, the Promenade, Colline du Château. Save your wallet for the food, not the view.

itinerary.title: Ready-Made Routes
itinerary.intro: If you hate planning, follow these flows. The times are flexible; keep the spirit, break the order.

plans.title: If You Have 1 Day
plans.subtitle: Market, old town, sea and sunset

steps.title: Cours Saleya market
steps.description: Walk among flower and fruit stalls; local fruit and an espresso count as breakfast.

steps.title: The lanes of Vieux Nice
steps.description: Get lost in the narrow streets: gelato on Place Rossetti, baroque churches, light between the washing lines.

steps.title: Socca break
steps.description: Hot socca from the wood oven + a glass of cold rosé. Nice's most honest lunch.

steps.title: Colline du Château
steps.description: Walk up (the lift doesn't count): the waterfall, the ceramic viewpoint and the best photo of the city.

steps.title: Sea hour
steps.description: Towel on the pebbles, dive into the Mediterranean. Feeling brave? Head toward Coco Beach and swim with the locals.

steps.title: Promenade sunset + dinner
steps.description: Sunset from the famous blue chairs, then a Vieux Nice bistro: pissaladière, daube, a glass of Bellet.

plans.title: If You Have 3 Days
plans.subtitle: Live the city as a guest, not a tourist

steps.title: The Nice classics
steps.description: The 1-day flow above: market, old town, hill, sea.

steps.title: Cimiez and art
steps.description: The Matisse Museum and the Cimiez monastery gardens in the morning, the Chagall Museum in the afternoon, fish near Le Port at night.

steps.title: A coastal escape and goodbye
steps.description: Take the train to Villefranche-sur-Mer or Èze; a pâtisserie crawl in the Musiciens quarter on return, and one last pan bagnat at night.

phrases.title: The 5-Word Survival Kit
phrases.intro: French courtesy words open doors in Nice; a pinch of Nissart wins smiles.

items.meaning: Hello — the mandatory first word of every exchange; skip it and the service turns cold
Please — add it to the end of your order
Cheers! — rosé glasses rise to this
'Long live Nice!' in Nissart — the city's chant, from the stadium to the street
